prompt: Why can't classical assert-based tests fully cover an LLM-powered feature?

options.text: Model outputs are probabilistic and often open-ended: many phrasings are correct, so exact-match assertions are the wrong instrument for quality

explanation: The testing discipline survives but the mechanics evolve: datasets + graders + aggregate scoring replace single expected strings. (Code checks still cover the checkable parts.)

prompt: A prompt tweak fixes the example you were debugging. The essential step before shipping is…

options.text: …running the full regression eval: prompt changes shift behavior globally, and fix-one-break-five is the default failure mode
…shipping immediately; one fixed example proves improvement

explanation: 'Looks better on my example' is how systems rot. The regression set is the only thing that sees the whole distribution.

prompt: The most valuable ongoing source of eval dataset examples is…

options.text: …production failures and human corrections: each one becomes a permanent regression case

explanation: The failure museum compounds: every fixed bug is guarded forever. Real traffic beats imagination; failures beat successes.

prompt: After weeks of tuning against the same 50 eval examples, scores are excellent but users still complain. This is…

options.text: …overfitting to the eval set: the same disease as tuning on the test set; refresh from traffic and keep a held-out slice

explanation: Every peek optimizes for the peeked-at set. Module 5's split discipline applies to prompts and pipelines exactly as it did to models.

prompt: The correct order for choosing graders is…

options.text: …exhaust cheap code checks (schema, length, citations, forbidden content), use reference comparison where gold answers exist, and reserve LLM judges for genuinely open-ended criteria
…LLM judges for everything; they're most sophisticated

explanation: Cheapest-sufficient-instrument first. A surprising share of 'quality' is deterministically checkable, and free checks run on every commit.

prompt: Before trusting an LLM judge, you must…

options.text: …measure its agreement against human grading on a labeled sample, and fix the rubric/judge prompt until agreement is high (~85–90%+)
…verify it uses the largest available model
…ensure it grades on a 1–100 scale for precision

explanation: A judge is a probabilistic system with known biases (length, position, self-family preference). Human agreement is its accuracy metric; without calibration it automates your blind spots.

prompt: A user reports a wrong answer. The trace shows correct chunks retrieved but an answer contradicting them. The fix belongs in…

options.text: …generation (grounding prompt/model), and the case joins the eval set permanently

explanation: Traces localize: context right, faithfulness wrong ⇒ generation-side fix. Localize → fix → immortalize as a regression case.

prompt: Why do latency SLOs use p95/p99 rather than the mean?

options.text: Averages hide the tail: a healthy mean coexists with 1-in-20 requests being painfully slow, and those define the experience users remember
p99 is always lower than the mean

explanation: Tail latency is the unlucky user's reality. Distributions, not points: the same statistical honesty as everywhere else in this course.

prompt: The human-correction rate in your review queue doubles over two weeks with no deploys. The most likely story is…

options.text: …drift: the input distribution shifted (new formats, segments, or an upstream/provider change): investigate recent traces against older ones

explanation: Quality proxies moving without deploys = the world moving under the model. Change-based alerts on correction/abstention rates are your earliest drift detectors.

prompt: What belongs in every stored trace? Select all that apply.

options.text: Version stamps: prompt version, model ID, config
Unredacted API keys and full customer PII for completeness

explanation: A trace must answer 'what exactly produced this?': stages, versions, costs. Secrets and unnecessary personal data are redacted: traces are a liability surface too.

prompt: 'Can the cheaper model handle our classification step?' The professional way to answer is…

options.text: …run both models on the eval set and compare scores, cost, and latency: minutes of compute replaces weeks of opinion
…always use the biggest model to be safe

explanation: Evals are the decision engine for model tiering. This is why teams with evals iterate boldly and cheaply.

prompt: Why gate releases on critical criteria rather than a single average quality score?

options.text: Averages can rise while rare critical behaviors (faithfulness, abstention) regress: the gate must watch the failures that actually hurt
Averages are too hard to compute
Gates are only for classical software

explanation: One rising mean can hide a hallucination regression on 5% of cases. Score criteria separately; block on the consequential ones.

prompt: In pairwise A/B judging, why must the order of the two candidates be randomized per comparison?

options.text: LLM judges show position bias (favoring one slot); randomization prevents the bias from systematically inflating one system
Alphabetical order is unfair to system Z

explanation: Known judge biases (position, length, self-family preference) get engineering mitigations: randomize order, grade criteria separately, calibrate against humans.

prompt: The economic argument for exhausting code-check graders before LLM judges is…

options.text: …code checks are free, deterministic, and run on every commit: spending judge tokens on what a regex could verify wastes money and adds noise
…there is no argument; always use judges

explanation: Cheapest sufficient instrument, always: schema validity, citation presence, forbidden content, and length are deterministic questions with deterministic answers.

prompt: A sensible release-gate policy for evals is…

options.text: …block on regressions in critical criteria (faithfulness, safety, abstention); allow judgment calls on minor aggregate movements, with the failure list reviewed either way
…block on any metric moving at all

explanation: Gates need teeth where harm lives and flexibility where noise lives. Criteria-level gating (not one average) is what makes that possible.

prompt: Traces must be redacted before storage because…

options.text: …they capture full prompts and outputs (including personal data and secrets) making the observability store itself a breach surface and retention liability
…raw traces are too large to store
…they mustn't be; full fidelity always wins

explanation: Observability and privacy collide in traces. Redact secrets and unneeded PII at capture; you cannot leak what you didn't keep (Module 15).

prompt: Offline evals and canary deployments are complementary because…

options.text: …evals catch anticipated failure classes pre-release; the canary catches the unanticipated in production with a small blast radius: neither substitutes for the other

explanation: Two nets at different heights: known-unknowns offline, unknown-unknowns online-but-bounded. Mature teams run both on every meaningful change.

prompt: Why version eval datasets like code?

options.text: Scores are only comparable against the same dataset version: an 87% on today's set versus 85% on last month's set is not an improvement claim, and audits need to reconstruct exactly what was measured
Datasets are too small to matter
To prevent anyone from adding cases

explanation: The dataset is half the measurement instrument. Version it, and note which version every reported score came from, or comparisons are apples to oranges.

prompt: Human corrections from production review queues are the richest quality signal because…

options.text: …they are continuous, labeled, real-traffic ground truth: every correction is a solved failure case ready to become an eval example

explanation: The review queue is an eval-data factory. Systems that harvest it improve continuously; systems that discard it re-learn failures the hard way.

prompt: A judge scores answers 'helpful: 8.7/10' on average. What's the methodological weakness?

options.text: Fine-grained scalar scales are noisy and drift-prone for LLM judges; binary or 3-point criteria-specific judgments calibrate better against humans and produce actionable failures
Helpfulness cannot be judged at all
The average should be a median

explanation: Ask judges narrow, checkable questions such as 'does the answer cite a source for the refund claim?' instead of requesting a broad subjective score. Precise questions produce more interpretable measurements.
